Description: This encompasses all functions of the kidney, including maintenance of acid-base balance; regulation of fluid balance; regulation of sodium, potassium, and other electrolytes; clearance of toxins; absorption of glucose, amino acids, and other small molecules; regulation of blood pressure; production of various hormones, such as erythropoietin; and activation of vitamin D.
Synonyms: Kidney, Renal function
BISAC_name_1: SCIENCE / Life Sciences / Anatomy & Physiology (see also Life Sciences / Human Anatomy & Physiology)

Description: The liver plays a role in nearly every organ system in the body. It interacts with the endocrine and gastrointestinal systems by aiding in digestion and metabolism. The liver is the storage location for fat-soluble vitamins and handles cholesterol homeostasis. It stores iron and copper.
Synonyms: Liver physiology
BISAC_name_1: SCIENCE / Life Sciences / Anatomy & Physiology (see also Life Sciences / Human Anatomy & Physiology)

Description: Muscle physiology is the branch of physiology that studies the function, mechanisms, and regulation of muscle tissue. It includes the processes underlying muscle contraction, such as the interaction of actin and myosin and the roles of calcium ions and ATP, as well as the neuromuscular junction, where motor neurons transmit signals to muscle fibers. Muscle physiology also encompasses different muscle types (skeletal, cardiac, and smooth) and examines how muscles respond and adapt to stimuli such as exercise, injury, and disease.
Synonyms: Muscle physiology, Muscle contraction
BISAC_name_1: SCIENCE / Life Sciences / Anatomy & Physiology (see also Life Sciences / Human Anatomy & Physiology)

Description: The function of the digestive system is to digest and absorb food and then excrete the waste products with the help of the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, small intestine, large intestine, and rectum. Each of these organs plays a specific role in the digestive system.

Synonyms: Buddhist teachings, Buddhist doctrine, Buddhist principles, Buddhist beliefs

Description: The Philosophy of Feelings is a branch of philosophy that examines the nature and role of human feelings, including emotions, affective states, and subjective experiences. It investigates questions concerning the origin, ontology, phenomenology, and ethical implications of feelings.
Synonyms: Philosophy of Emotions, Affective Philosophy, Ethics of Emotion
German Synonyms: Philosophie der Emotionen, Philosophie der Gefühle

Description: The mind–body problem is a debate concerning the relationship between thought and consciousness in the human mind, and the brain as part of the physical body.
Pragmatisim is a tradition rooted in 19th and early 20th century American philosophy and is characterized by its theorization from lived experience.
Synonyms: Practicalism, Instrumentalism, Utilitarianism, Experimentalism

Description: Neo-Kantianism refers to a philosophical movement that emerged in the late 19th and early 20th centuries as a reinterpretation and development of Immanuel Kant's ideas. It sought to update Kant's philosophy in light of new developments in science, logic, and philosophy itself.
Synonyms: Neo Kantianism, New Kantianism

Description: Materialism is a philosophical perspective that posits that the physical or material world is the fundamental reality, and that all phenomena, including mental states and consciousness, can ultimately be explained in terms of material or physical processes. Materialists assert that everything, including thoughts, emotions, and consciousness, can be reduced to and explained by the interactions of matter and physical forces.
Synonyms: Physicalism, Naturalism, Scientism, Physical Realism

Description: Empiricism is the thesis that knowledge is derived from experience. Empiricism is a philosophical approach that emphasizes the importance of sensory experience and empirical evidence as the foundation for acquiring knowledge and understanding the world. It holds that knowledge originates primarily from observation, experimentation, and direct sensory experience, rather than relying on innate ideas or theoretical speculation. Empiricists believe that knowledge can be gained through the senses, and they often seek to validate or refute hypotheses through observable evidence and data.
Synonyms: Empirical method, Sensationalism, Positivism
THEMA_name_1: Philosophy: epistemology and theory of knowledge

Description: Speech act theory is a branch of pragmatics and the philosophy of language that explores how utterances function not only to convey information but also to perform actions. It investigates the communicative acts performed by speakers through their use of language and the ways in which language is used to accomplish various actions.
Synonyms: Illocutionary Acts, Perlocutionary Acts, Locutionary Acts, Speech Act Classification
DDC_name_2: Psychological principles, language acquisition, speech perception

Description: Analytical philosophy of language is a specific subfield within the philosophy of language that focuses on the philosophical analysis of language using logical and analytical methods. It emerged primarily in the 20th century and is associated with the tradition of analytic philosophy.
Synonyms: Logical Analysis of Language, Semantics and Pragmatics, Language and Logic

Description: Continental Philosophy refers to non-Anglophone European philosophy of the 20th and 21st centuries (primarily phenomenology, existentialism, poststructuralism, postmodernism, deconstruction, critical theory, and Marxism) and Anglophone philosophy that engages primarily with that body of work.
DDC_name_1: Modern western and other noneastern philosophy
THEMA_name_1: Philosophical traditions and schools of thought

Description: Analytic philosophy is analyzes the use of language (linguistic turn) and, by clarity and rigor in its arguments, it focusses on solving philosophical questions. It contributes and utilizes formal logic and mathematics, and, to a lesser degree, the natural sciences.
Synonyms: Linguistic Philosophy

Description: German Idealism refers to a philosophical movement that emerged in Germany in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. It is characterized by a focus on the nature of consciousness, reason, and the relationship between mind and reality. German Idealism was a response to the Enlightenment and its emphasis on empirical science and rationalism. The central ideas and themes of German Idealism include: Transcendental idealism, Subjectivity and self-consciousness, Absolute idealism, Systematic philosophy.
Synonyms: Classical German philosophy, Idealism of the German tradition, Kantian Idealism, Post-Kantian Idealism, Transcendental Idealism
DDC_name_1: Idealism and related systems and doctrines

Description: Naturalism, in the social sciences and humanities, refers to a philosophical outlook that emphasizes the importance of empirical observation, analysis, and explanation, advocating for the use of scientific methods and the investigation of causality in understanding human behavior, culture, and society.
Synonyms: Physicalism
DDC_name_1: Naturalism and related systems and doctrines

Description: Conceptual analysis is a philosophical methodology used to investigate the meaning and nature of concepts. It involves breaking down a concept into its constituent parts and examining how they relate to one another. The goal of conceptual analysis is to gain a deeper understanding of concepts and clarify their meanings, often in the context of philosophical or theoretical discussions.
Synonyms: Conceptual inquiry, Conceptual investigation, Conceptual scrutiny, Conceptual examination, Conceptual evaluation

Description: Experimental philosophy is an interdisciplinary approach that combines philosophical inquiry with empirical research methods from psychology, cognitive science, and other disciplines. It seeks to investigate philosophical questions by gathering empirical data through experiments, surveys, and other empirical techniques, rather than relying solely on traditional philosophical methods such as conceptual analysis or logical argumentation.
Synonyms: Empirical philosophy, X-Phi, Philosophical empiricism, Philosophical experimentation, Empirically informed philosophy
LCC_name_1: Philosophy. Methodology. Relation to other topics

Description: The "history of philosophy as method" refers to an approach in philosophical inquiry where the study of the history of philosophy is seen as a methodological tool for engaging with philosophical questions. Rather than viewing the history of philosophy as a separate discipline or a mere historical survey, this approach considers it as an active and integral part of philosophical investigation.
Synonyms: Historical approach to philosophy, Historical-philosophical method, Philosophical historiography, Philosophical inquiry through history, Historical contextualization in philosophy
THEMA_name_1: Philosophical traditions and schools of thought

Description: Logical analysis refers to the systematic examination and evaluation of arguments and propositions using the principles and methods of logic. It involves breaking down complex statements or arguments into their logical components to assess their validity, soundness, consistency, and coherence. Logical analysis aims to uncover the logical structure of a statement or argument and determine whether it follows valid reasoning.
Synonyms: Logical examination, Logical evaluation, Logical investigation, Logical reasoning, Logical assessment

Description: Philosophy of Sociology examines the foundational questions and theoretical frameworks of sociology, exploring the nature of social phenomena, knowledge, and methodologies.
LCC_name_1: Relation to social sciences. Relation to sociology

Description: Numismatics is the study of coins, currency, and related objects, including their history, production, and cultural significance.
Sphragistics, also known as sigillography, is the study of seals and signets, including their history, design, and use in authenticating documents and objects.
Heraldry studies the design and display of armorial bearings (known as armory).
Synonyms: Coat of Arms

Description: Chronology is the science of arranging events in their order of occurrence in time. It contains the methods, and systems of dating historical events, measuring the passage of time. Historiography can thus define temporal relationships between different occurrences.
Genealogy is the study of family history and lineage, tracing the ancestry and descent of individuals and families through historical records and genetic information.
Diplomatics is a scholarly discipline centred on the critical analysis of documents – particularly, but not exclusively, historical documents.

Disability Pedagogy is the study and practice of inclusive teaching approaches that recognize disability as a form of human diversity, aiming to remove barriers and promote equitable learning for all students.
THEMA_name_1: Teaching of students with physical impairments or disabilities

Description: Gifted education (also known as gifted and talented education (GATE), talented and gifted programs (TAG), or G&T education) is a sort of education used for children who have been identified as gifted and talented.  The main approaches to gifted education are enrichment and acceleration. An enrichment program teaches additional, deeper material, but keeps the student progressing through the curriculum at the same rate as other students.  Special education (known as special-needs education, aided education, exceptional education, alternative provision, exceptional student education, special ed., SDC, or SPED) is the practice of educating students in a way that accommodates their individual differences, disabilities, and special needs. This involves the individually planned and systematically monitored arrangement of teaching procedures, adapted equipment and materials, and accessible settings. These interventions are designed to help individuals with special needs achieve a higher level of personal self-sufficiency and success in school and in their community, which may not be available if the student were only given access to a typical classroom education.
Synonyms: GAT
BIC_name_1: Teaching of specific groups & persons with special educational needs
LCC_name_1: Exceptional children and youth. Special education
THEMA_name_1: Teaching of students with different educational needs

Description: Experiential education is an approach to learning that emphasizes direct engagement with real-world experiences as a means of acquiring knowledge, skills, and attitudes. It involves active participation, reflection, and application of learning in practical contexts, going beyond traditional classroom-based instruction.
Synonyms: Hands-on learning, Active learning, Learning by doing

Description: Assessment and testing are two related concepts in the field of education that focus on evaluating and measuring students' knowledge, skills, and understanding. Although they are interconnected, they have distinct meanings and purposes. Assessment refers to the ongoing process of gathering evidence and information about students' learning progress, achievements, and areas of growth. Testing, on the other hand, refers to a specific form of assessment that involves measuring students' knowledge and skills through standardized or formalized assessments.
Synonyms: Evaluation Measurement Appraisal Examination
DDC_name_1: Examinations and tests; academic prognosis and placement
LCC_name_1: Educational tests, measurements, evaluations and examinations

Description: Holistic education is an approach to learning that considers the whole person, focusing on the development of individuals intellectually, emotionally, socially, physically, and spiritually. It aims to cultivate well-rounded individuals who can thrive in various aspects of life and contribute positively to society. Holistic education goes beyond the traditional emphasis on academic achievement and incorporates a broader range of skills, values, and qualities.
Synonyms: Integrated education, Whole-person education, Comprehensive education

Description: Intermediality, in other words, is not only the general term that defines the relationships between autonomous media, it is also the term that identifies the internal plurality of each medium. The intermedial study of literature therefore does not only refer to the study of the relationships between the literary text and its “others” (for instance the illustrations that accompany it, to give an elementary example), it also includes the study of the literary as a heterogeneous material that conveys a more or less radical “semiotic rupture” within itself (for instance when we interpret aspects of typography, from typeface to page layout and book design, as aspects of the text’s visuality—a dimension of literature that has always been at the center of visual and experimental poetry).

Though "classical music" is the vernacular term, the more accepted academic term is "concert music" or "Western art music." Description: Contemporary music typically refers to avant-garde art music of the late 20th and early 21st century; it is sometimes called "New Music."

Auditing is a systematic and independent examination of an entity's financial statements, records, and other relevant information to provide an opinion on their accuracy and reliability. The primary objective of auditing is to enhance the credibility of financial information provided to stakeholders by identifying and addressing material misstatements, errors, and fraud.  In research, auditing involves the development and testing of theories related to the audit process, audit quality, and the impact of auditing on financial reporting and decision-making. The field of auditing research covers a wide range of topics, including audit risk, audit evidence, audit regulation, auditor independence, and audit market competition.  Audit risk refers to the risk that the auditor will issue an incorrect opinion on an entity's financial statements, which could result in stakeholders making incorrect decisions based on unreliable information. Audit evidence refers to the information used by the auditor to support their opinion on the accuracy and reliability of an entity's financial statements.  Audit regulation refers to the rules and standards that govern the conduct of auditors and the performance of audits. Auditor independence refers to the ability of the auditor to provide an objective and unbiased opinion on an entity's financial statements, free from any conflicts of interest or undue influence.  Audit market competition refers to the level of competition among audit firms and how it affects audit quality and pricing.  In practice, auditing involves the examination of an entity's financial statements and records, the testing of internal controls, and the evaluation of management's representations. The auditor uses various techniques and procedures, including sampling, analytical procedures, and substantive testing, to gather sufficient and appropriate evidence to support their opinion.  Auditing is typically performed by certified public accountants (CPAs) who are independent of the entity being audited. The result of an audit is typically a report that includes the auditor's opinion on the accuracy and reliability of the entity's financial statements.

Description: Business Information Systems (BIS) is a field of study that focuses on the effective and efficient use of technology and information systems to support the operations, management, and decision-making processes of businesses. BIS combines elements of computer science, management science, and business administration to develop and implement systems that improve business performance.  Some of the major topics in BIS include:  Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP): ERP systems integrate and automate key business processes, such as accounting, inventory management, and customer relationship management.  Customer Relationship Management (CRM): CRM systems are used to manage customer interactions and improve customer satisfaction and loyalty.  Supply Chain Management (SCM): SCM systems optimize the flow of materials, information, and finances across the supply chain to improve efficiency and reduce costs.  Business Intelligence and Analytics: BIS helps businesses to collect and analyze data to support decision-making processes.  E-commerce: E-commerce systems enable businesses to conduct transactions online and reach a global audience.  Knowledge Management: Knowledge management systems help businesses to capture, store, and share knowledge and expertise within the organization.  Cybersecurity: BIS focuses on the protection of business information systems from cyber threats, such as hacking and data breaches.  Overall, BIS aims to align technology with business goals and objectives to create a competitive advantage for the organization.
Synonyms: MIS, Management Information Systems

Description: Oral health refers to the health of the teeth, gums, and the entire oral-facial system that allows us to smile, speak, and chew. Some of the most common diseases that impact our oral health include cavities (tooth decay), gum (periodontal) disease, and oral cancer. Oral conditions are frequently considered separate from other chronic conditions, but these are actually inter-related. Description: Licensing refers to the legal process of granting permission to use an intellectual property (IP) asset such as a patent, trademark, or copyright to a third party in exchange for compensation, usually in the form of royalties or fees. Licensing is an important field of research and practice within technology commercialization because it enables companies to monetize their inventions and innovations while avoiding the costs and risks associated with manufacturing and distribution. The core topics of licensing as a field of research and practice within technology commercialization include: Intellectual Property Law: Licensing is a legal process, and thus a fundamental understanding of intellectual property law is essential for practitioners in this field. This includes knowledge of the different types of IP assets, the requirements for obtaining and maintaining them, and the legal frameworks that govern their use and enforcement.  Negotiation and Contracting: Licensing agreements involve complex negotiations and contractual agreements between the licensor and the licensee. Practitioners must be skilled in drafting and negotiating these agreements, as well as understanding the key terms and provisions that are critical to the success of the licensing deal. Technology Assessment: Before licensing a technology, it is important to assess its commercial viability and potential market demand. Practitioners must be able to evaluate the technology's potential market size, competitive landscape, and potential applications to determine whether it is a viable candidate for licensing. Market Analysis: To successfully license a technology, practitioners must have a deep understanding of the market and the competitive landscape. This includes conducting market research, identifying potential licensees, and developing a licensing strategy that aligns with the company's overall business goals. Intellectual Property Valuation: Determining the value of an IP asset is critical in negotiating licensing agreements. Practitioners must be able to accurately assess the value of the IP asset, taking into account factors such as the strength of the patent, the size of the market, and the potential revenue streams. Compliance and Enforcement: Once a licensing agreement is in place, it is important to ensure that both parties comply with the terms of the agreement. Practitioners must be able to monitor and enforce compliance, and take legal action when necessary to protect the licensor's rights and interests. Overall, licensing is a complex field that requires a deep understanding of intellectual property law, negotiation and contracting, technology assessment, market analysis, intellectual property valuation, and compliance and enforcement.

Queueing theory is a field of management research and practice that focuses on the study of waiting lines, or queues, and the mathematical models used to analyze them. The goal of queueing theory is to understand the behavior of queues, how to design systems that minimize wait times and improve efficiency, and how to make informed decisions regarding system improvements and resource allocation.  Queueing theory considers various factors that impact queue performance, such as the arrival rate of customers or requests, the service rate of the system, the number of servers or service points available, and the behavior of customers while they wait. By analyzing these factors, queueing theory provides managers and analysts with the tools to optimize system performance, identify bottlenecks, and evaluate system trade-offs.  Queueing theory has broad applications in many fields, including telecommunications, transportation, healthcare, finance, and manufacturing. It is used to design call centers, hospitals, factories, and other systems that require efficient resource utilization and customer service. In addition, queueing theory is also used to study the behavior of customers and employees, providing insights into their decision-making processes and the factors that influence their behavior.

Description: Software Management is a field of business and management research and practice that focuses on managing the development, delivery, and maintenance of software products and services. Project Management: This involves the planning, organizing, and managing of resources to achieve specific software development goals within a given time frame and budget.  Software Testing: This involves the process of evaluating software products or services to ensure they meet quality standards and user requirements.  Software Maintenance: This involves the ongoing process of updating and improving existing software products or services to ensure they remain functional and relevant.  Software Metrics and Measurements: This involves the use of quantitative data to measure and track the progress of software development projects and assess their success.  Software Quality Assurance: This involves the process of ensuring that software products or services meet established quality standards and requirements.  Risk Management: This involves identifying, assessing, and managing risks that could impact the success of software development projects.  Software Architecture: This involves the design and organization of software components and systems to ensure they are scalable, maintainable, and meet user requirements.  Team Management: This involves managing software development teams to ensure they are effective and efficient in achieving project goals.

Description: Tokamaks are devices that use a powerful magnetic field to confine a hot plasma in the shape of a torus. The tokamak is one of several types of magnetic confinement devices being developed to produce controlled thermonuclear fusion power and it is the leading candidate for a practical fusion reactor.

RNA editing is the process by which ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules are enzymatically modified post synthesis on specific nucleosides. Examples of RNA editing include pseudouridylation (the isomerization of uridine residues) and deamination (removal of an amine group from cytidine to give rise to uridine, or C-to-U editing).

Description: Sodium (Na, atomic number 11) is an alkali metal that exists in living systems as Na+ ions. In physiology, it regulates blood volume, blood pressure, osmotic equilibrium and cellular pH. Description: Enterprise Architecture (EA) is a field of business and management research and practice that focuses on the design and implementation of a coherent and integrated set of business and IT capabilities that support an organization's goals and objectives. It involves the development of a comprehensive understanding of an organization's current and desired states, and the identification of the gaps and opportunities for improvement.  The following are major topics within the field of Enterprise Architecture:  Business Architecture: Business Architecture defines the organization's business strategy, goals, processes, and organizational structure. It aims to provide a clear understanding of the organization's operations and how they can be optimized.  Information Architecture: Information Architecture defines the organization's information strategy, including the data, information, and knowledge assets required to support the business processes. It ensures that information is available, secure, and usable by the organization's stakeholders.  Application Architecture: Application Architecture focuses on the design and implementation of software applications that support the organization's business processes. It includes the development of application standards, guidelines, and best practices.  Technology Architecture: Technology Architecture defines the organization's technology strategy, including the hardware, software, and network infrastructure required to support the business processes. It ensures that the technology is aligned with the organization's goals and objectives.  Governance: Governance refers to the establishment of policies, standards, and procedures to ensure that the Enterprise Architecture is consistent with the organization's goals and objectives. It ensures that the organization's resources are used effectively and efficiently.  Change Management: Change Management refers to the process of managing the changes to the Enterprise Architecture. It involves the development of a plan to manage the implementation of new systems, applications, or processes, and the communication of the changes to stakeholders.  Risk Management: Risk Management involves identifying, assessing, and managing risks associated with the implementation of the Enterprise Architecture. It ensures that the organization's assets are protected and that the risks are managed effectively.  Overall, the goal of Enterprise Architecture is to provide a holistic and integrated view of the organization, its processes, and its resources.

Description: Financial engineering is a multidisciplinary field that applies mathematical and quantitative methods to design, develop, and analyze financial products, instruments, and strategies. In research and practice, financial engineering involves a range of activities and tasks, including:  Design and development of financial products: The design and development of financial products such as derivatives, options, and futures contracts, which can be used to manage financial risk or to achieve specific investment objectives.  Risk management: The identification, assessment, and management of financial risks associated with various financial products and strategies, including credit risk, market risk, and operational risk.  Quantitative analysis: The use of mathematical and statistical models to analyze financial data and to develop strategies for managing financial risk.  Optimization of financial strategies: The development and optimization of financial strategies such as portfolio management, asset allocation, and hedging strategies, to achieve specific financial objectives such as maximizing returns or minimizing risk.  Pricing and valuation: The development of pricing and valuation models for financial products, to ensure that they are priced accurately and fairly.  Overall, the goal of financial engineering is to create innovative financial products and strategies that meet the needs of investors and financial institutions, while managing financial risk and achieving specific financial objectives. In practice, financial engineering is used by a range of financial institutions and organizations, including banks, hedge funds, insurance companies, and pension funds.

Description: Patenting is a field of management research and practice that focuses on the strategic use of patents to commercialize technology. This field encompasses a range of topics related to the identification, acquisition, management, and enforcement of patents in order to create value for a firm.  Core topics within the field of patenting include:  Patent strategy: This topic focuses on developing a patent strategy that aligns with a firm's overall business goals. It involves understanding the competitive landscape and identifying areas where patents can be used to create a competitive advantage.  Patent acquisition: This topic deals with the process of acquiring patents either through internal development or external sources, such as licensing or purchasing patents from other firms. It includes assessing the value of patents and negotiating licensing or acquisition agreements.  Patent portfolio management: This topic involves managing a firm's patent portfolio to maximize its value. It includes identifying and prioritizing patents for commercialization, monitoring the patent landscape for potential infringement, and assessing the potential value of new patents.  Patent litigation: This topic deals with the legal aspects of enforcing patents, such as filing lawsuits against infringers or defending against infringement claims. It includes assessing the likelihood of success in litigation and the potential costs and benefits of pursuing legal action.  Patent licensing: This topic involves negotiating licensing agreements with other firms to commercialize patented technology. It includes assessing the value of the licensed technology, negotiating licensing terms, and monitoring compliance with the licensing agreement.  Overall, patenting is a critical field for firms looking to commercialize technology, and understanding its core topics is essential for success in this area.

Description: Business Process Management (BPM) is a discipline within the field of management and information technology that focuses on designing, modeling, executing, monitoring, and optimizing business processes. BPM seeks to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of business operations by aligning them with the strategic goals of an organization. Major topics within BPM include: Process modeling: This involves documenting and representing business processes using diagrams and other visual aids. Process modeling helps stakeholders to understand the flow of activities, inputs, and outputs in a process, and to identify potential bottlenecks and inefficiencies. Process automation: This involves using technology to automate routine or repetitive tasks within a process. Process automation can help to reduce errors, improve consistency, and free up human resources to focus on more complex or strategic activities. Process optimization: This involves identifying areas for improvement within a process and implementing changes to streamline and improve its performance. Process optimization can help to reduce costs, increase customer satisfaction, and improve overall business performance. Process monitoring: This involves tracking the performance of a process over time, using metrics and other indicators to identify trends and areas for improvement. Process monitoring can help to identify bottlenecks, inefficiencies, and other issues that may be affecting the performance of a process. Process governance: This involves establishing policies, procedures, and guidelines for the management of business processes within an organization. Process governance helps to ensure that processes are consistent, compliant, and aligned with the strategic goals of the organization. Process innovation: This involves exploring new and innovative ways to design, execute, and manage business processes. Process innovation can help to drive business growth, create competitive advantage, and improve overall organizational performance.

X-ray scattering is a technique used to study the structure and properties of materials at the atomic and molecular levels. By analyzing the scattering pattern, valuable information about the atomic arrangement, crystal structure, and other properties of the material can be obtained.  Two main types of X-ray scattering techniques: X-ray Diffraction (XRD), Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS).
Synonyms: X-ray Diffraction (XRD), X-ray Crystallography, X-ray Reflectivity, X-ray Scattering Analysis

Synonyms: Ribosomes

Description: Palliative care is the set of medical interventions to alleviate symptoms, most frequently pain, associated with a medical condition. The main goal of palliative care is to reduce and prevent patient suffering. Unlike therapeutics, palliative care does not aim to cure the underlying disease. Palliative care is an interdisciplinary medical caregiving  approach that improves the quality of life of patients and their families facing the problems associated with life-threatening illness, through the prevention and relief of suffering by means of early identification and impeccable assessment and treatment of pain and other problems, physical, psychosocial, and spiritual.

Industrial psychology, also known as industrial-organizational psychology or I-O psychology, is a field of psychology that focuses on understanding and improving human behavior in the workplace. It applies psychological principles and research methods to address issues related to personnel selection, employee training and development, organizational effectiveness, and work environment. Industrial psychology aims to enhance employee well-being, productivity, and job satisfaction while optimizing organizational performance and efficiency.

Market psychology, also known as investor psychology or financial psychology, refers to the study of how psychological factors influence financial markets, investment decisions, and market behavior. It explores the role of emotions, cognitive biases, and social influences in shaping market trends, investor sentiment, and the overall functioning of financial markets.

The term Mental Training is used to describe a variety of psychological methods, which aim at facilitating and improving performance, resilience, self-awareness, confidence or well-being by optimising social and communicative skills, cognitive skills or motivational and emotional processes.   In Sport Psychology, the narrow definition of Mental Training specifies it as training procedures for optimising the regulation of movement by conciously and repeatedly envisioning movement tasks or actions. Mental Training may also include techniques to regulate emotion (anger, fear, stress), motivation (will, achievement motivation) or perception (focus, concentration) and strengthen the athletes confidence in his or her capability. This may also include techniques that focus on coach-athlete or team interaction. Besides the long term systematic application of mental training, it is also used situationally in competition preparation or evaluation.

Attention deficit disorder (ADD), as a field of study in psychology, focuses on understanding the nature, causes, and treatment of attention deficits that significantly impact individuals' daily functioning. It involves examining the cognitive, behavioral, and emotional aspects of attention difficulties, as well as exploring the factors that contribute to the development and persistence of attention deficits. Researchers and clinicians in the field of ADD aim to identify effective strategies and interventions to help individuals with attention deficits improve their attentional control, academic performance, and overall well-being.

Substance abuse addiction, also known as substance use disorder, is a field of study in psychology that focuses on understanding and addressing the patterns of excessive and harmful use of substances such as drugs or alcohol. It involves examining the psychological, social, and biological factors contributing to the development and maintenance of addiction, as well as developing effective prevention, intervention, and treatment strategies. The field of substance abuse addiction seeks to understand the underlying mechanisms, risk factors, and consequences associated with substance abuse, and to promote recovery and overall well-being.

Psychotic Disorder, as a field of study in psychology, focuses on understanding and treating severe mental illnesses characterized by significant disturbances in thinking, perception, and behavior. Researchers and clinicians in this field investigate the causes, symptoms, and treatment options for psychotic disorders, such as schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. They examine biological, psychological, and social factors that contribute to the development and progression of these disorders, and work towards developing effective interventions to alleviate symptoms and improve overall functioning.

Panic Disorder, as a field of study in psychology, focuses on the examination and treatment of a type of anxiety disorder characterized by recurrent and unexpected panic attacks. Researchers and clinicians in this field explore the etiology, risk factors, and underlying mechanisms of panic disorder, including biological, psychological, and environmental factors. They investigate the cognitive and physiological processes involved in panic attacks, assess the impact of panic disorder on daily functioning and well-being, and develop effective interventions for symptom management and recovery.

Agoraphobia, in the context of psychology, refers to a specific anxiety disorder characterized by an intense fear or anxiety about being in situations or places where escape might be difficult or help may not be readily available in the event of a panic attack or other distressing symptoms. Individuals with agoraphobia often avoid or feel significant distress in places such as open spaces, crowded areas, public transportation, or places outside their comfort zone. Agoraphobia is a field of study within psychology that focuses on understanding the causes, symptoms, assessment, and treatment of this particular anxiety disorder.

Social phobia, also known as social anxiety disorder, is a psychological condition characterized by intense fear and anxiety in social situations. Individuals with social phobia often experience excessive self-consciousness and a fear of being judged or humiliated by others. This fear can significantly impact their ability to engage in social interactions and can lead to avoidance behaviors. The field of study that examines social phobia and its related aspects is known as social psychology.

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a field of study within psychology that focuses on understanding and addressing the psychological and emotional impact of traumatic experiences. It involves the exploration of the symptoms, causes, and treatment of PTSD, which can occur following exposure to a traumatic event such as war, natural disasters, accidents, or personal assault. Researchers and practitioners in this field aim to better understand the complex nature of PTSD, its effects on individuals, and develop effective interventions to promote healing and recovery.

Somatoform Disorder is a field of study in psychology that involves the investigation and understanding of a group of mental disorders characterized by physical symptoms that cannot be fully explained by a medical condition or other physiological factors. Individuals with somatoform disorders often experience distress and impairment due to their physical symptoms, which are believed to be influenced primarily by psychological factors.

Eating disorders, as a field of study in psychology, involves the examination of abnormal eating behaviors and their psychological underpinnings. Researchers and clinicians in this field investigate the complex interplay between biological, psychological, and sociocultural factors that contribute to the development and maintenance of eating disorders. They study various types of eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge eating disorder, aiming to understand the underlying mechanisms, risk factors, and treatment approaches associated with these conditions. The field of eating disorders encompasses research, assessment, and interventions to support individuals struggling with disordered eating patterns and promote their recovery.

Sexual disorders refer to a range of conditions that affect an individual's ability to experience sexual arousal, desire, or function in a way that is satisfactory to them. These disorders can have a significant impact on an individual's quality of life and relationships. The field of study that focuses on the diagnosis, assessment, and treatment of sexual disorders is known as sexual psychology.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is a widely used therapeutic approach within the field of psychology that focuses on the connections between thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. It is based on the idea that our thoughts and beliefs influence our feelings and behaviors, and by identifying and modifying negative or maladaptive thought patterns, individuals can experience positive changes in their emotions and behaviors. CBT combines cognitive restructuring techniques to address faulty thinking patterns with behavioral techniques to promote behavioral change and improve overall well-being.

Operant conditioning, in the field of psychology, is a form of learning in which behavior is influenced by its consequences. It involves the use of reinforcements (rewards or punishments) to strengthen or weaken a specific behavior, thereby shaping and modifying behavior over time.

Social learning, in the field of psychology, refers to the process by which individuals acquire new behaviors, attitudes, or knowledge through observation, imitation, and interaction with others in their social environment. It emphasizes the role of social interactions and modeling in shaping behavior and cognitive processes.

Achievement motivation refers to the psychological drive or desire to accomplish and succeed in challenging tasks, activities, or goals. It is a field of study within psychology that focuses on understanding the factors that influence individuals' motivation to achieve success, excel in their endeavors, and attain desired outcomes. Achievement motivation encompasses various cognitive, emotional, and behavioral processes that contribute to goal-directed behavior and the pursuit of excellence. Researchers in this field explore topics such as goal setting, self-evaluation, self-regulation, persistence, and the impact of achievement motivation on academic, occupational, and personal achievement. The study of achievement motivation aims to enhance our understanding of the complex factors that drive individuals to strive for success and the ways in which motivation can be fostered and optimized.

Power motivation can manifest in different ways, such as seeking leadership roles, striving for control and dominance, or exerting influence over others to achieve personal or group goals.

Group coaching is a type of coaching that involves working with a group of individuals who share a common goal or interest. In this approach, a coach facilitates a group session in which each participant has the opportunity to share their experiences, insights, and challenges related to the group's focus. The coach supports the group by providing structure, guidance, and feedback to help members achieve their individual and collective goals.

The coach provides guidance, support, and feedback to help individuals improve their job performance, achieve their career goals, and reach their full potential.  In coaching, the coach and employee work together to identify areas for improvement and set goals for development. The coach may use a variety of techniques, such as questioning, active listening, and role-playing, to help the employee gain new insights and develop new skills.  Coaching is often used in conjunction with other Human Resources Management initiatives, such as performance management, talent development, and leadership development. Coaching can be provided by internal coaches within an organization, or by external coaches who are hired on a contract basis.

Description: Leadership psychology is a field of management research that focuses on understanding the psychological processes that underlie effective leadership. It seeks to identify the personality traits, cognitive abilities, and behavioral patterns that are associated with successful leadership, as well as the situational factors that influence leadership effectiveness.  Leadership psychology draws on a range of theories and research methods from psychology, sociology, and other social sciences to examine how leaders motivate and inspire others, build trust and loyalty, and navigate complex social dynamics. It also investigates the impact of leadership on organizational culture, employee satisfaction, and overall performance.  Research in leadership psychology has practical implications for management practice, as it can help organizations identify and develop effective leaders, as well as design training and development programs to improve leadership skills at all levels of the organization. It also informs policies and practices that promote ethical leadership, diversity and inclusion, and employee well-being.

Performance feedback: This involves providing employees with information about their performance and ways to improve. Performance improvement plans: This involves creating plans for employees who are not meeting performance standards, outlining the steps they need to take to improve. Goal setting: This involves setting specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART) goals that align with the organization's objectives. Coaching and mentoring: This involves providing employees with guidance and support to help them develop their skills and achieve their goals. Succession planning: This involves identifying and developing employees who have the potential to take on leadership roles within the organization. Overall, performance development and management is essential for improving employee performance, increasing employee engagement, and achieving organizational goals.

Description: Personnel selection is the process of evaluating job candidates and making decisions about who to hire for a particular job. It is a crucial part of human resource management and involves various methods and techniques to assess the knowledge, skills, and abilities of candidates. The main goal of personnel selection is to identify the most qualified candidate for a job while ensuring fairness and objectivity in the selection process. Topics within personnel selection include: Job analysis: This involves identifying the knowledge, skills, and abilities required for a specific job and developing job descriptions. Recruitment: This involves attracting a pool of qualified candidates for a job through various sources such as job postings, social media, and employee referrals. Screening: This involves reviewing resumes, conducting initial phone interviews, and assessing whether candidates meet the minimum requirements for the job. Selection tests: These can include cognitive ability tests, personality tests, and job simulation exercises to assess a candidate's knowledge, skills, and abilities. Interviews: These can be structured or unstructured and can involve behavioral questions or situational questions to assess a candidate's fit for the job. Background checks: These involve verifying a candidate's education, work history, and other relevant information. Decision making: This involves evaluating all the information gathered during the selection process and making a decision about which candidate to hire. In research, personnel selection is a well-studied area of organizational psychology and human resource management. Researchers investigate the effectiveness of different selection methods and techniques, the fairness and validity of selection processes, and the impact of personnel selection on employee outcomes such as job satisfaction and performance.
Synonyms: Staffing, Recruitment, Talent acquisition, Candidate selection, Employee selection, Hiring process, Personnel assessment

Description: Cognitive dissonance, in the field of psychology, refers to the psychological discomfort or tension that arises from holding conflicting beliefs, attitudes, or values, or from engaging in behaviors that contradict one's beliefs or self-image. When individuals experience cognitive dissonance, they are motivated to reduce the discomfort by altering their beliefs, attitudes, or behaviors to restore consistency.

The Milgram Experiment, conducted by social psychologist Stanley Milgram in the 1960s, aimed to examine the willingness of individuals to obey authority figures, even when their actions may harm others. The study involved participants acting as "teachers" who were instructed to administer electric shocks to a "learner" whenever they answered a question incorrectly. In reality, the shocks were fake, and the learner was an actor. The experiment revealed the significant influence of authority and situational factors on human behavior. It demonstrated that a considerable number of participants were willing to administer potentially harmful shocks to others simply because they were instructed to do so by an authority figure. The findings raised ethical concerns regarding the well-being of participants and the power of authority in shaping human behavior.

Description: Megakaryocytes are large, multinucleated cells found in the bone marrow that are responsible for the production of platelets (thrombocytes), which are essential for blood clotting. These cells originate from hematopoietic stem cells and undergo a process called endomitosis, where they replicate their DNA without cell division, resulting in a large cell with multiple nuclei. Once mature, megakaryocytes extend cytoplasmic projections called proplatelets into the bloodstream, which fragment into individual platelets. Megakaryocytes play a crucial role in hemostasis, the process that prevents excessive bleeding, and are also involved in various physiological and pathological processes, including inflammation and immune responses.
Synonyms: Megakaryocyte

Description: Diversity Management is a field of research and practice that focuses on promoting diversity and inclusion in the workplace. It involves recognizing and valuing differences in individuals based on their race, gender, age, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, and other dimensions of diversity. Diversity management aims to create an inclusive workplace culture where all employees feel valued, respected, and supported, and where they can contribute their unique perspectives and experiences to the organization's success.  As a field of research, diversity management investigates the factors that influence diversity in the workplace, such as hiring practices, leadership styles, and organizational culture. It explores the impact of diversity on organizational outcomes such as performance, innovation, and employee well-being. Research in this field also examines strategies for managing diversity, such as diversity training programs, mentorship and sponsorship initiatives, and employee resource groups.  Women in Business is a field of research and practice that focuses on advancing women's leadership and career development in business and management. It seeks to address the barriers that women face in the workplace and promote gender equality in leadership positions. Women in Business aims to create a more diverse and inclusive workplace where women have equal opportunities to advance and succeed.  As a field of research, Women in Business investigates the factors that contribute to gender inequality in the workplace, such as unconscious bias, stereotypes, and systemic barriers. It explores strategies for promoting gender equality and advancing women's leadership, such as mentorship and sponsorship programs, flexible work arrangements, and inclusive leadership practices. Research in this field also examines the impact of women's leadership on organizational outcomes, such as performance, innovation, and employee engagement.  As a field of practice, Women in Business involves implementing programs and initiatives that support women's leadership and career development, such as leadership development programs, networking events, and advocacy campaigns. It also involves creating a supportive organizational culture that values diversity and inclusion and fosters the advancement of women in the workplace.
Synonyms: DEI

Description: The Five Factor Model (FFM), also known as the Big Five personality traits, is a widely accepted framework in psychology that organizes human personality into five broad dimensions: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism (commonly referred to as OCEAN). Description: Viral reservoirs refer to populations of viruses that persist in a host organism or environment, often in a dormant or low-activity state, allowing them to evade the host's immune response and antiviral treatments. Description: Heart development, also known as cardiogenesis, is the complex biological process through which the heart forms and matures from embryonic structures. This process begins in the early stages of embryonic development, typically around the third week of gestation in humans, and involves a series of tightly regulated events including cell differentiation, migration, and morphogenesis. Key stages of heart development include the formation of the heart tube, looping of the heart tube to establish the basic heart structure, and the septation of the heart chambers to create a four-chambered organ. Fugu (also known as Takifugu), commonly referred to as pufferfish, is a genus of fish belonging to the family Tetraodontidae, notable for their ability to inflate their bodies and for containing potent toxins, particularly tetrodotoxin. The species Fugu rubripes, also known as the Japanese pufferfish, is significant in scientific research due to its relatively small genome and has been a model organism in genomic and evolutionary studies. Its genome was one of the first among vertebrates to be sequenced, providing insights into vertebrate evolution and genetics. Fugu is also culturally important in Japanese cuisine, where it is prepared as a delicacy, requiring specialized training to serve safely due to its toxic properties.
Synonyms: F. rubripes, T. rubripes, Torafugu, Takifugu, Takifugu rubripes, Fugu rubripes

introversion is a personality trait characterized by a focus on internal thoughts and feelings, rather than on external stimulation and interaction with others. Introverts tend to be reflective, reserved, and more comfortable with solitude than socializing. They may prefer quieter environments and may feel overwhelmed by large groups or excessive stimulation. Introversion is often contrasted with extroversion, which is characterized by a focus on external stimulation and social interaction. It is important to note that introversion is not the same as shyness or social anxiety, although introverts may experience these conditions.

Description: Sport Kinematics is the study of the spatial and temporal expression of motion in sport. Kinematics is the study of the geometric and time-dependent aspects of motion. Neutron diffraction or elastic neutron scattering is the application of neutron scattering to the determination of the atomic and/or magnetic structure of a material. Lymphangiogenesis is the biological process through which new lymphatic vessels are formed from pre-existing lymphatic vessels. This process is crucial for maintaining fluid homeostasis, immune responses, and tissue repair. Lymphangiogenesis is regulated by various growth factors, notably Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor-C (VEGF-C) and VEGF-D, which stimulate the proliferation and migration of lymphatic endothelial cells. It plays a significant role in pathological conditions such as cancer metastasis, where tumor cells can exploit lymphatic vessels for dissemination, as well as in chronic inflammatory diseases and lymphedema. Understanding lymphangiogenesis is essential for developing therapeutic strategies aimed at modulating lymphatic function in various diseases.
Synonyms: Lymphangiogenesis

Description: Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory disease of the gastrointestinal tract, mostly affecting the ileum. Synonyms: Nonlinear Phenomenon

Description: Chromatin structure describes the physical structure of chromatin within the eukaryotic nucleus and how structure affects chromatin processes such as transcription. Description: Hepatorenal syndrome is defined as renal failure in patients with advanced liver disease - liver cirrhosis, ascites and liver failure - in the absence of existing kidney disease or structural kidney abnormalities. The condition is a serious complication and can be life-threating; typical signs are reduced renal blood flow and vasculature constriction.
